title: SLAs-to-Savings: field hypotheses and test notes
content:
Goal: craft short, testable field claims that ties latency SLAs to measurable per-customer cost savings. This doc is a set of working hypotheses, proposed experiments, and suggested customer-facing phrasings for sales + demo teams. Not final — rough numbers pulled from lab results and early Dedicated customer telemetry.

Context and why this matters
- Common buyer problem: product teams trade latency for cost unpredictability. They ask: how will maintaining a 200–300ms median improve conversion/retention and what does that do to my per-session cost?
- Our advantage: smart batching + KV/prefix caching + model variants + routing policies let Redwood hit tighter median latency at materially lower token-per-second cost compared to naïve single-instance endpoints.
- Messaging gap: field teams need crisp, testable claims that map SLA -> $/MAU or $/100K sessions.

High-level hypotheses (to validate in pilots)
1) 200ms p50 SLA reduces perceived UI friction and increases feature engagement by ~8–12% for short-turn chat flows (<= 40 tokens produced). This increased engagement offsets additional marginal infra spend and yields net revenue lift per 100k sessions.
2) Switching from unbatched 1:1 endpoints to Redwood’s continuous batching+cache profile reduces per-token inference cost by 24–37% on typical Q&A workloads (median sequence length 64 tokens).
3) Using regional routing + fallback variants can hold p95 latency under a 1s SLO while allowing 15–20% lower reserved capacity commitments (capex equivalent savings for Dedicated customers).

Concrete proof points we can gather (metrics and experiments)
- Metric set to capture in pilot: p50/p90/p95 latency (generation), tokens per request, mean tokens/sec consumed, cost per 1k tokens (hosted unit pricing), sessions to conversion, avg session length
- Experiment A (PLG customer): enable Redwood batching + KV cache on a chat feature for 2 weeks, A/B vs current provider. Measure engagement lift, compute delta $/100k sessions using observed tokens/session * unit price.
- Experiment B (Dedicated enterprise): run traffic with default routing vs aggressive region+variant fallback for 7 days. Measure reserved GPU utilization, observed p95, and compute projected committed capacity reduction.

Sample numbers (lab -> rough field proxies)
- Typical short chat: 28 tokens produced, 12 tokens prompt. Lab p50: 180 ms, p95: 320 ms. Competitor baseline (multi-tenant endpoint, no cache): p50 420 ms, p95 950 ms.
- Cost delta: at 1M tokens/month, Redwood observed $78/month vs competitor $102 (about 24% saving) when batching and prefix caching are in play for this workload shape.
- Burst amortization note: for session-heavy workloads, session-level KV cache saved ~9–14% of tokens across repeated calls which compounds savings over MAU.

Customer scenarios and tailored claims (short, testable)
- Small PLG startup (chat onboarding): "Keep first-response latency under 250ms — customers stay inside flows 9% longer; our runtime reduces your inference bill by ~25% for chat workloads of this size." (Caveat: numbers based on 40-token median workloads; we'll include an asterisk in collateral linking to benchmark details)
- Marketplace with multimedia summaries: "Maintain p95 < 1s worldwide using regional routing and fallback — reduce required committed capacity by up to 20% vs static single-region deployments." (Support with capacity model spreadsheets in linked artifacts)
- Enterprise customer (SaaS with strict SLA needs): "Pin a model and rollout policy — guaranteed 99.9% uptime and predictable p50 latency; opt-in batching policies reduce per-token spend while meeting your SLOs." (Operational controls + audit logs are the supporting product points)

Competitor notes (call-outs for objection handling)
- Competitor A (big cloud LLM service): often claims low median but under multi-tenant load p95 tails badly. Effective rebuttal: show p95 traces and our fallback behavior; emphasize predictable economics via Dedicated reservations.
- Competitor B (self-hosted runtimes): better raw latency for tuned on-prem stacks but high ops burden and poor autoscaling for bursts. Rebuttal: show demo of Redwood autoscaling + burst smoothing saving ops hours and lowering peak commit requirements.
- Competitor C (API-first small provider): cheaper on list price but lacks KV/prefix caching and continuous batching; their effective cost at scale rises due to repeated token generation for sessions.

Suggested field artifacts (what to give sales/solutions engineers)
- One-pager: "Latency to margin — quick calculator" with inputs: tokens/session, sessions/day, desired p50, current provider unit price. Output: projected monthly inference $ and % saving. (Spreadsheet + short script to run numbers live in demo)
- Scripted demo: two side-by-side sessions (competitor vs Redwood) for 30-second workflow, live token counts, live latency clock, and final cost estimate printed.
- Customer email template: 3-sentence claim + 1-sentence caveat + link to lab appendix and benchmarking workbook.

Proof plan and ownership
- Bench harness owner: Research/Applied ML (Noah Li) — maintain reproducible scripts, seed dataset, and variant configs.
- Field pilot owner: Solutions Engineering (Luis Gomez) — run 2 customer pilots by end of Q1 and collect required metrics.
- Sales enablement: Emma Rivers to create the quick calculator and 1-pager.

Open questions and risks (working list)
- How to normalize token price across model variants? We propose a normalized unit cost baseline: effective $/1k tokens for a given model-profile and a separate multiplier for quantization/variant differences.
- Risk: customers conflate p50 claims with experience for complex multi-turn flows — we need explicit segmentation language in collateral (short-turn vs long-form generation).
- Measurement drift: caching effectiveness depends heavily on user behavior patterns. Pilot should include session-level caching breakdown.

Next steps (short timeline)
- Week 0–2: finalize bench scripts, create demo recordings for short-turn and long-turn scenarios.
- Week 3–6: run 2 pilots (one PLG chat product, one Dedicated-bound enterprise). Capture telemetry and draft claim docs.
- Week 7: synthesize pilot results into "Latency-to-savings brief" (final) and produce the calculator + 1-pager.

Appendix: sample sales lines and rebuttals (short form)
- Opening claim (concise): "We reduce typical chat inference cost by ~25% while cutting median latency in half for short-turn flows."
- If buyer says "I only care about p95": "We tune our routing and fallbacks to hold p95 within your SLO — and the same policies let us reduce reserved capacity compared to single-region static deployments. We'll show you capacity models from a prior pilot."
- If buyer says "price is lower elsewhere": "Price lists don't capture effective cost — we include batching, cache, and session amortization in our demos so you see monthly delta for your workload shape."

Notes-to-self: keep phrasing concrete, avoid words like 'always' and 'guarantee' in early collateral. Add bootstrapped visual: p50/p95 bar charts + cost breakdown waterfall for 100k sessions. Link bench notebooks in artifacts before next review.
